items.title: 6.1.4 Equation of a Circle with Given End points of a Diameter

source_refs.note: Book p. 167: equation of the circle on the diameter with ends A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2) using the right angle in a semicircle, Figure 6.4; Do You Know? box

blocks.alt: Circle with centre O at the origin. A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2) are the ends of a horizontal diameter; P(x, y) is a point on the circle joined to A and B, with a right angle (90 degrees) marked at P.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: the angle APB in a semicircle is a right angle (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
Let \(A(x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \(B(x_{2}, y_{2})\) be the end points of the diameter. Let \(P(x, y)\) be any point on the circle. From plane geometry, the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is a right angle. Therefore,
\[\angle APB = 90^{\circ}\]
Thus, the lines \(\overline{AP}\) and \(\overline{BP}\) are perpendicular to each other.
The slope of \(\overline{AP}\) is \(m_{1} = \frac{y - y_{1}}{x - x_{1}}\) and the slope of \(\overline{BP}\) is \(m_{2} = \frac{y - y_{2}}{x - x_{2}}\).
Using the condition for perpendicularity of two lines, \(m_{1} \cdot m_{2} = -1\), we obtain:
\[\dfrac{y - y_{1}}{x - x_{1}} \cdot \dfrac{y - y_{2}}{x - x_{2}} = -1\]
Multiplying both sides by \((x - x_{1})(x - x_{2})\) gives:
\[(y - y_{1})(y - y_{2}) = -(x - x_{1})(x - x_{2})\]

blocks.text_alt: (x minus x1)(x minus x2) plus (y minus y1)(y minus y2) equals 0

blocks.text: This is the required equation of the circle.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(\angle APB = 90^{\circ}\)? This is the Class IX/X theorem 'the angle in a semicircle is a right angle'. So every point \(P\) of the circle sees the diameter \(AB\) at a right angle, and the perpendicularity condition \(m_{1}m_{2} = -1\) turns that fact into an equation.
The slopes are undefined when \(P\) coincides with \(A\) or \(B\) (or when \(\overline{AP}\) is vertical), but the final equation has no fractions and is still satisfied there: put \(x = x_{1}\), \(y = y_{1}\) and both products are zero. So the final equation includes every point of the circle.
Another way to the same circle: centre = mid-point of \(AB\), radius = half of \(|AB|\); then use the standard form. Both ways give the same equation.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: A circle has the maximum area for a given perimeter among all closed shapes.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own illustration (not from the book): the circle on the diameter with ends \(A(1, 2)\) and \(B(5, -4)\).
\[(x - 1)(x - 5) + (y - 2)(y + 4) = 0\]
\[x^{2} - 6x + 5 + y^{2} + 2y - 8 = 0\]
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 6x + 2y - 3 = 0\]
Check: centre \((3, -1)\) is the mid-point of \(AB\); radius \(\sqrt{9 + 1 + 3} = \sqrt{13}\) equals \(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{16 + 36} = \sqrt{13}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Circle on the diameter with ends \((x_{1}, y_{1})\), \((x_{2}, y_{2})\): \((x - x_{1})(x - x_{2}) + (y - y_{1})(y - y_{2}) = 0\).
2. It comes from the angle in a semicircle (\(90^{\circ}\)) and \(m_{1}m_{2} = -1\).
3. The centre is the mid-point of the diameter and the radius is half its length.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing the pairs: \(x\) goes with \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) and \(y\) with \(y_{1}, y_{2}\); never \((x - x_{1})(y - y_{1})\).
2. Sign errors with negative coordinates: end point \((5, -4)\) gives \((y + 4)\).
3. Writing \(= r^{2}\) on the right: the diameter form always has 0 on the right side.
